transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-09-27
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Priya (Sandstone Head of ML), Marcus (Infra Lead), Elena (Security)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): Discuss reserved capacity, isolation needs for PHI, warm pools and burst modeling, encryption/KMS and audit requirements, next step to run benchmarks.

[00:00] Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick intro — I'm Ava, AE here at Redwood, with Samir our SE and Lena on success. Sandstone, would you like to do a 30s intro?
[00:18] Priya (Sandstone): Yeah hi, I'm Priya, head of ML at Sandstone — we do genomics assay analysis and inference over sensitive patient derived data, so PHI is a hard requirement. Marcus is infra, Elena is security. We're evaluating options for reserved GPUs because we have predictable daytime bursts when pipelines run.
[00:35] Marcus (Sandstone): Our current job is basically bursty: 9am-1pm and 7pm-10pm windows, spikes up to ~120 concurrent requests, but they are short, like 10-30s per request. We need isolation to ensure tenant blast radius minimal because of regulatory crates.
[00:52] Samir (Redwood SE): Got it. That pattern maps well to a reserved pool plus a warm pool for fast prewarm. A few quick Qs: where do you need data residency and is on-prem an option?
[01:05] Elena (Security): Data stays in the US East region only. On-prem is under consideration for PHI but we'd prefer VPC/private deployment first. Also we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[01:20] Ava: Perfect — we'll note VPC + KMS. Quick note: we support both Dedicated reserved pools and a Private control plane. For PHI most customers pick Dedicated inside a VPC with customer-managed keys.
[01:34] Priya: Two important success criteria: latency under 300ms p50 for short queries, and throughput to handle the 120 concurrent without queueing, also cost per request needs to be predictable for budgeting.
[01:49] Samir: Ok, we generally achieve sub-200ms p50 for many open models on dedicated A100 variants with warm KV cache and prewarm; p95 is more variable. We'll want to profile your payloads — sequence lengths matter a lot.
[02:10] Marcus: Our payloads are JSON-wrapped sequences — average token length 120, but some long reports hit 850 tokens. We can sanitize and share distribution.
[02:23] Ava: Great, please do. On the isolation front: are you requiring single-tenant nodes or strict tenant fencing with no neighboring tenants?
[02:35] Elena: For the most sensitive workloads we want single-tenant GPUs or physical isolation — can't have co-tenants on the same card for certain pipelines. For lower-sensitivity jobs maybe soft isolation is ok.
[02:49] Samir: That's doable — we have dedicated node pools (single-tenant) and also multi-tenant but fenced via runtime isolation and quotas. Single-tenant carries a cost premium and affects how we provision warm pools.
[03:06] Priya: About warm pools — how quickly can the model be hot for our 10-30s inference? We need near-zero cold start to keep that 300ms SLO.
[03:15] Samir: There are two levers: kernel-level prewarming and KV prefix cache warmup. For short calls the common trick is to keep a small hot pool (a handful of prewarmed processes) and use continuous batching to combine requests. That keeps per-request latency low but costs more.
[03:32] Marcus: Do you support burst to hosted as a fallback if reserved is exhausted? For example during an unpredicted spike.
[03:39] Ava: Yes we can route overflow to compatible hosted variants with a policy toggle; it's commonly used as graceful degradation. Usually customers configure cost-tiered fallbacks to keep critical traffic alive.
[03:51] Elena: On audits — we need all inference logs (no raw PHI) and access logs forwarded to our SIEM and key rotation records from KMS. Is that instrumented?
[04:02] Samir: We have audit log ingestion hooks and KMS/HSM integrations. Note: audit logs can redact payload bodies by default on PHI flows, but you can request additional retention.
[04:15] Priya: What's the typical api contract for billing and reserved commitments? We want to compare to our EC2 reserved cost.
[04:25] Ava: Reserved capacity is monthly/annual commits by GPU-equivalent units. Billing includes base reserved fee plus variable token usage. We'll send a worksheet with modeled costs for your profile.

[05:00] Speaker 2: (background) yeah
[05:15] Samir: Let's sketch a sizing exercise live — if you expect 120 concurrent, what is per-GPU concurrency for your preferred model?
[05:24] Priya: For our tuned open model we measured 12 concurrent connections per A100 80GB for p50 250ms if KV cache warm, p95 increases, but with quantized variants we can get more concurrency.
[05:40] Samir: Ok that implies ~10-12 GPUs as base to handle peak, plus buffer. For warm-pool prewarm we recommend 15% of the pool kept hot to absorb sudden spikes.
[05:55] Marcus: How about eviction and preemption? We run long batch jobs overnight that can be preempted but daytime inference must be sacrosanct.
[06:05] Samir: We support node labels and scheduling policies that reserve a set for daytime inference, and allow batch to fill remaining capacity at night. Preemption policies are configurable.
[06:16] Lena (CSM): From an onboarding perspective, we often do a quick synthetic benchmark: you send a representative payload set, our SE runs a 2-hour run in a mirrored env, we return lat/throughput metrics and suggested reserve.
[06:28] Priya: That sounds good — Melanie? (laughter) — Priya actually. We'll plan to sanitize and send sample traces.

[07:00] [7:00] Marcus: On network — do you support private peering into our VPC, or is it a managed VPC where we accept peering?
[07:12] Samir: For Dedicated we support VPC peering and Private control plane. For on-prem we have an appliance option but that's heavier. Most PHI customers choose VPC + KMS.
[07:24] Elena: For KMS — do you support HSM-backed keys and customer-managed key rotation?
[07:30] Samir: Yes, we integrate with common KMS providers and support bring-your-own-key with HSM. Rotation events and usage are logged and can be exported.
[07:40] Ava: Any hard timeline requirements?
[07:43] Priya: We want to start a pilot in November; procurement needs a security pack and an initial SOW for budget approval by mid-October.
[07:53] Ava: We'll aim to get the security pack and draft SOW this week, send the pricing worksheet by Oct 6.

[08:20] Priya: A few technical nitty-gritty: can we pin model versions for rollouts and have automatic fallback to a quantized variant if the primary fails?
[08:31] Samir: Yes, rollouts and model pinning are supported. We can configure runtime fallbacks and variant routing by policy. The fallback model must be compatible in interface.
[08:42] Marcus: How much profiling detail do you need to estimate token cost? We have a spread: short 120 tokens (60% of calls), medium 400 tokens (30%), long 800+ (10%).
[08:55] Samir: That distribution is perfect — we'll use it for cost modeling. Also note that batching patterns and sequence length skew changes effective throughput.
[09:10] Elena: Encryption at rest: where are images, model weights stored? Are those encrypted with our KMS?
[09:18] Samir: Model weights on-disk in Dedicated are encrypted at rest; you can request that image volumes are encrypted with your CMK. We can offer HSM attestation where required.

[09:45] Ava: Let's talk about SLA — what's non-negotiable for you?
[09:49] Priya: Uptime during working windows with an error budget that allows for brief maintenance outside those windows. And a clear incident escalation path to a named support engineer.
[09:58] Lena: Our enterprise plans include an SRE on-call and a lead SE for escalations. We can put SLOs in the contract for critical windows.
[10:10] Marcus: Are there recommended guardrails for cost control if we route overflow to hosted? E.g., token caps, throttles?
[10:18] Samir: Yes, we can set token budget caps, route only non-critical traffic to hosted, and have circuit breakers to prevent runaway costs.

[11:00] Priya: Any limitations on prewarming quantized models? We plan to try int8 quantized variants for cost, but worried about quality regression on edge-case reports.
[11:09] Samir: Quantized models reduce memory and increase concurrency, but quality impacts vary. We recommend running A/B evals on your prompt set; Redwood Optimize can surface regressions tied to prompt sets.
[11:25] Priya: Good — we'll want the quality monitoring tied to the release so we know if quantization changed outputs.
[11:33] Ava: We'll include Optimize trial in the pilot recommendation.

[12:00] [12:00] Elena: For legal/procurement: do you offer SOC2 + ISO artifacts and the option to get an AICPA attestation?
[12:09] Ava: Yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 packs are available; for enterprise we can facilitate a security questionnaire and a redaction-safe artifact share.
[12:21] Elena: Ok please send the full pack and our procurement will do a review. Also send sample contract language for data handling.

[13:00] Samir: Very practical question — latency from our NYC cluster to your US-East region — do you have a region preference?
[13:08] Priya: Primary in us-east-1 please. We can run a single region for now.
[13:12] Samir: Great. We'll include a latency estimate for the chosen region in the benchmark report.

[14:00] Marcus: If we do single-tenant nodes, how will update windows work? We can't have sudden restarts mid-run.
[14:08] Samir: We coordinate maintenance and provide scheduled windows; we can do live node migration in some cases but usually customers schedule rolling updates during low-traffic windows.
[14:20] Priya: For the pilot, can we get a temporary dedicated pool for 2 weeks? We'll try the full workload.
[14:27] Ava: Yes — we can provision a short-term dedicated eval pool for benchmark with agreed limits. That's usually done as a paid pilot.

[15:00] [15:00] Lena: I'll coordinate the pilot logistics and calendar. Proposed: 2-hour synthetic benchmark then a 48-hour pilot for real traffic, costed.
[15:11] Priya: Sounds good. We'll need a statement of work for budget signoff.
[15:16] Ava: We'll draft SOW and pricing.

[16:00] Marcus: Anything about rate limits per tenant? We have internal rate limiters.
[16:06] Samir: We support per-API-key/QPS limits, token rate limits, and route-level quotas. These can be set per-tenant or per-route.
[16:18] Elena: Final question: can we audit the instance firmware/driver versions? We have strict controls and need to attest drivers for GPGPU.
[16:26] Samir: We can provide a list of driver/kernel versions; for Dedicated we can offer attestation screenshots at provisioning. There's an additional compliance process for locked-down environments.

[17:00] Ava: OK let's recap next steps: Redwood send security pack + SOC2 by Oct 1; Sandstone to share sanitized payload distribution by Oct 4; Redwood SE runs benchmarking plan and returns suggested reserve sizes and a pricing worksheet by Oct 6; schedule pilot week of Oct 11. Anyone object?
[17:22] Priya: No objections.
[17:25] Marcus: Good.
[17:27] Elena: We'll review the security pack with procurement.
[17:30] Ava: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and create the calendar invites for the benchmarking run.
[17:36] (call ends)

Transcript notes (noise/imperfections): Occasional speaker mislabels (Speaker 2) and faint background talk at ~05:00. Some words auto-transcribed (KMS vs K-M-S, KV cache transcribed as kayvee cache).
